articles.title: Spanish economist to become new European Central Bank chief
articles.summary: Economist Pablo Hernandez de Cos was announced after a meeting of eurozone leaders.
articles.body:
The president of the European Council says eurozone member states have agreed to recommend Pablo Hernandez de Cos as the new European Central Bank (ECB) president.

Antonio Costa also announced that Laurence Boone and Markus Brunnermeier have been recommended as members of the ECB executive board, and noted that this paves the way for the formal appointment of the new European Central Bank leadership by December’s European Union summit.

Pablo Hernandez de Cos will become the first Spaniard to take the role, and succeeds France’s Christine Lagarde at the Frankfurt-based institution at a challenging time for the eurozone.

Currently head of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS), the Basel-based forum for the world’s major central banks, the 55-year-old will take over in February, when Lagarde would step down several months before her term expires in October next year.

Thursday’s green light triggers a formal process during which European leaders will later in the day approve the candidates for each ECB post. The bank’s governing council and European Parliament will then formally back the nominations.

Diplomats have described the Spanish economist as a “steady hand” to steer the institution, with a reputation for pragmatism and consensus-building.

As the Bank of Spain’s chief economist and later governor, he navigated the aftermath of Spain’s 2010s banking crisis, years of ultra-low inflation, COVID-19 and the 2022 inflation surge that followed the pandemic and Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

He also chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, the global standard-setter for banks.

Spain’s Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez, who is battling unfavourable polling before a general election on Sunday, hailed the choice on social media, saying it reflects “a Spain that leads in Europe”.

He pointed to the Spanish chief of the European Investment Bank, Nadia Calvino, and the EU executive’s second-most senior official, Teresa Ribera, as other figures of influence.

articles.title: Two Italians killed by ‘drone strike debris’ in Kuwait
articles.summary: Iran has strongly denied any involvement in the fatal incident.
articles.body:
Two Italians have died from their injuries in Kuwait, after being hit by falling debris as authorities said they tried to intercept incoming Iranian drones.

Kuwait’s Ministry of Defence said two other workers, a Kuwaiti and a Pakistani national, were also wounded in the incident, at what the ministry describes as a “vital site”.

However, Iran’s foreign minister Abbas Araghchi held a phone conversation with his Kuwaiti counterpart Jarrah Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, denying Tehran’s involvement and saying Tehran was prepared to conduct a “joint investigation with the Kuwaiti side” into the incident, state TV reported.

“During the call, Araghchi firmly rejected allegations regarding an Iranian drone attack on Kuwait, stating that the Islamic Republic of Iran had no involvement whatsoever,” it said.

Iran’s military spokesman Sardar Shekarchi said there had been “no offensive or military operations in the region”, and said that “given the history of hostile actions and the role of the Zionist regime and American forces in using false flags and regional adventures, these accusations are considered a cover for continuing evil and an attempt to increase insecurity in the region”.

Italy’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs and International Cooperation confirmed its citizens’ deaths, saying, “an explosion caused by a drone attack … occurred at a site where two Italian technicians from the company Rheinmetall Italia were working,” with Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani confirming the victims were technicians working at an air-defence surveillance station.

“Regarding the targeting of a vital site in the country as a result of the heinous Iranian aggression, the two injured Italian nationals have died as a result of their injuries,” said Kuwait’s Defence Ministry. It had earlier said the injured were taken to a hospital for treatment while the incident caused unspecified “material damage”.

Al Jazeera’s Zein Basravi said the Iranian drone attack happened while the Kuwaiti National Guard and Kuwaiti military were meeting with an Italian delegation that was visiting, including the commander general of the Italian Carabinieri, Lieutenant-General Salvatore Lungo, as well as the Italian ambassador to Kuwait.

Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said she was informed of the “tragic deaths”.

“On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims’ families,” Meloni wrote on X.

The countries of the Gulf region “have in one voice said an attack against one is an attack against all and have continued to condemn these attacks as a violation of sovereignty”, but we’ve seen an uptick in attacks since September, said Basravi, reporting from Doha.

Jasem Mohamed Albudaiwi, secretary-general of the Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC), strongly condemned Thursday’s “brutal” attack.

In a statement, Albudaiwi stressed that Iran’s continued attacks on Kuwait, targeting its vital facilities and endangering the lives of civilians, constitute a dangerous escalation and threaten regional security.

There was no immediate comment from Iran regarding the attack.

But it was in line with Tehran’s “policy change”, said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from the Iranian capital.

“Increasingly we have heard from the Iranian officials … saying that this state of no war, no peace cannot remain in place forever, and Iran is working on some military options … to break the status quo,” said Serdar.

The conflict – which began with US-Israeli strikes on Iran in late February – has seen the Gulf states caught in the crossfire, with US military facilities and energy installations on their soil targeted.

The United States and Iran are in a standoff over the vital Strait of Hormuz, with the US military working to escort ships transiting the waterway in defiance of Tehran’s attempts to close the strait.

Thursday’s deadly attack comes days after Kuwait activated its air defences to counter drone strikes launched by Iran – the first since early September.

articles.title: India's answer to drone swarms? Bhargavastra clears key trials
articles.summary: India's indigenous counter-drone system Bhargavastra has completed its development trials at the Pokhran field firing ranges in Rajasthan.
articles.body: India's indigenous counter-drone system Bhargavastra has completed its development trials at the Pokhran field firing ranges in Rajasthan. The trials demonstrated its ability to engage drone swarms using air defence rockets and guided micro-missiles.According to news agency ANI, Solar Defence and Aerospace Limited (SDAL) conducted the trials between November 20 and 24. The tests involved firing rockets and guided micro-missiles at actual swarm-drone targets to assess the system's ability to detect, track and neutralise multiple aerial threats.The trials assessed the system's ability to engage actual swarm-drone targets. The Rocket warheads successfully hit their designated points. Separate tests also demonstrated the guidance and terminal-homing capabilities of the micro-missiles against drone targets.The trials further evaluated the integration of sensors, surveillance radars and the command-and-control network for detecting and tracking incoming drones.ANI reported that further optimisation and trials are planned to improve the system's engagement and kill probability. The next milestone is a prototype demonstration in its deliverable configuration.Bhargavastra systemDeveloped by Solar Defence and Aerospace Limited (SDAL), Bhargavastra is an indigenous, vehicle-mounted, two-layer counter-swarm drone system designed to detect, track and destroy multiple hostile unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), including coordinated drone swarms and loitering munitions.The system uses a hard-kill approach, physically destroying incoming threats rather than relying solely on electronic jamming. It combines two weapon configurations. Version-I features a 64-tube launcher firing unguided air-defence micro-rockets, while Version-II uses a 64-micro-missile launcher equipped with autonomous guidance and infrared (IR) seekers for precision engagement.The system integrates surveillance radars, passive radio-frequency (RF) detectors and electro-optical/infrared (EO/IR) sensors to identify and track incoming aerial threats.Its radar can detect small aerial targets at distances of 6 to 10 km, while the electro-optical tracking system has a reported range of around 6 km.An artificial intelligence-enabled Command, Control, Communications and Intelligence (C4I) network integrates sensor inputs, tracks targets and coordinates weapon engagement.The system is designed for deployment across different terrains, including high-altitude areas above 5,000 metres. Its modular architecture can also accommodate an additional soft-kill layer involving electronic jamming and spoofing.Bhargavastra's significance lies in its ability to provide a layered response to the growing threat of low-cost drone attacks.Modern battlefields have increasingly seen coordinated drone swarms used to overwhelm air-defence networks, target military installations and strike critical infrastructure.The system's unguided micro-rockets are designed to counter groups of incoming drones, while guided micro-missiles provide a precision-engagement option against individual targets. This could help reduce dependence on expensive air-defence interceptors against relatively inexpensive drones.The system has been developed under the Indian Army's Make-II programme, with SDAL independently developing the guided micro-missile version beyond the initial rocket-based requirement.

articles.title: Top Russian aerospace commander arrested on corruption charges
articles.summary: Russia ​has arrested the deputy commander of its aerospace forces on suspicion of corruption, in a case that follows lapses in its air ⁠defenses.
articles.body: Russia ​has arrested the deputy commander of its aerospace forces on suspicion of corruption, media reported on Thursday, in a case that follows major lapses in its air ⁠defenses, including Ukraine’s bombing of the bridge linking Russia and Crimea. Col. Gen. Yuri Grekhov was placed in pre-trial detention by a military court, according to an online case record. It did not specify the ⁠charge against him but ​business ⁠news outlets Kommersant and RBC were among those to report the corruption allegation, which RBC said he denied. Grekhov, ⁠64, is a former commander of the Air and ​Missile Defense ⁠forces, who in his ‌latest role was responsible for ensuring the adequate provision of aircraft, missile defense systems and other weaponry. Several of Russia’s influential ‌war bloggers linked the arrest to air ‌defense failures including the repeated Ukrainian bombing of the Crimean Bridge, which knocked out its road section while leaving its rail portion intact. One of ⁠the blogs, Fighterbomber, reported that another deputy aerospace commander had also been summoned for a reprimand. With front lines on the battlefield largely static, both Russia and Ukraine have resorted increasingly to long-range air strikes on military, energy and commercial targets as the war approaches the end of its fifth year. Ukraine ‌has inflicted heavy blows this year on Russian ​oil refineries, causing them to greatly reduce output. ‌On Tuesday it said it had ⁠struck a major Russian military air base, damaging five ⁠planes used to launch missiles and bombs at Ukraine. Since the war ‌began, Russia has ​launched a series of corruption ‌investigations against senior defense officials, resulting ​in several long jail terms.

articles.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed: Has the holiday tradition ever been canceled?
articles.summary: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade was postponed by a powerful coastal storm, but the New York City tradition has been canceled only three times.
articles.body: While severe weather forced the 100th Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade to postpone until Saturday for the first time ever, the holiday tradition has only been canceled three times in its century-long history — a three-year hiatus for World War II. New York City officials announced Wednesday evening that this year's march would move to Saturday, Nov. 28 at 8:30 a.m. as a powerful coastal storm brings heavy rain and damaging wind gusts between 60 mph and 70 mph to the Northeast and New England, according to FOX Weather. Forecasts projected Thursday morning gusts between 35 mph and 45 mph, exceeding safety limits requiring sustained winds below 23 mph and gusts under 34 mph for balloons to fly. Even when severe weather threatened past parades, organizers historically kept the march moving on Thanksgiving Day, grounding all the giant balloons only once, in 1971, when heavy rain and high winds kept the inflatables deflated while floats and marching bands continued down the route, according to FOX5 New York. The city's current wind limits were adopted after the 1997 parade, when 40 mph gusts blew the "Cat in the Hat" balloon into a lamppost and injured spectators. A LOOK AT HOW THE TRUMPS SPEND THEIR THANKSGIVING HOLIDAY THROUGH THE YEARS To find the only years the parade was canceled altogether, you have to step back more than eight decades to the World War II home front. Following the Dec. 7, 1941, attack on Pearl Harbor, American factories shifted to wartime production, and critical supplies like rubber and helium were needed for the military. For three straight years — 1942, 1943 and 1944 — Macy's canceled the Thanksgiving Day march so its materials could support the war effort. Rather than issuing a dry corporate notice, Macy’s ran a 1942 newspaper advertisement written from the perspective of its grounded balloons, according to the American Rosie the Riveter Association. "We Macy balloons have always stood for peace and plenty of fun for all," the advertisement read. "We were a weaving and bobbing symbol of democracy at play. We figured in a parade devoted to laughter and shenanigans. Fear never marched in our ranks." "But now we’ve a war to win and we’ve enlisted, to help make the world safe for future parades full of merriment and good will," the ad continued. On Nov. 13, 1942, Macy's Jack Strauss formally donated the giant balloons to New York City Mayor Fiorello La Guardia and the New York City Salvage Committee, according to Macy's and The New York Times. During a dramatic City Hall ceremony, La Guardia dressed as St. George and symbolically slayed an air-filled, 60-foot dragon balloon with a knife, converting the parade stars into 650 pounds of scrap rubber bound for military tires, life rafts or dirigibles. CENTCOM'S THANKSGIVING MESSAGE TO TROOPS 'IS ONE OF DEEP GRATITUDE' FOR THEIR 'EXCEPTIONAL WORK' PROTECTING US Canceling the march also conserved helium, metal cylinders, tires and gasoline while freeing up New York police officers to guard warehouses and docks instead of managing a 2-million-person crowd, Macy's noted at the time. Even with the streets quiet, the department store kept some holiday magic alive with its mechanical window displays designed by Russell Patterson, which opened at 9 a.m. on Thanksgiving Day with a 26-float show titled "The Funny Page Parade." When the parade finally returned in 1945, the pent-up excitement turned the route down Central Park West from 106th Street to Herald Square into what The New York Times described as a second victory parade. An estimated 2 million spectators lined the streets, including more than 30,000 people packed into Times Square. "For the generation born during the war it was the opening of a new wonderland," The New York Times reported at the time. Seven bands and 20 floats marched past a large model of the Statue of Liberty in Times Square as NBC broadcast the event on television for the very first time. Helium-filled giants returned to the Manhattan skyline, including a 45-foot "Bobo" holding 6,600 cubic feet of helium, a 40-foot teddy bear, a triple-scoop ice cream cone and a 16-foot aerialist swinging from a 25-foot balloon that required occasional top-offs of helium along the route when its head began to sag. Since that triumphant 1945 comeback, the march has rolled on through other national crises until this week's storm. In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, there was no audience along the parade route and organizers cut down the march from two blocks to one.

articles.title: How a teen’s death raises questions about Colombia’s security crackdown
articles.summary: President Abelardo de la Espriella’s campaign against armed groups has resulted in accusations of extrajudicial killing.
articles.body:
Bogota, Colombia – On the afternoon of September 13, Marelvis Rodriguez said goodbye to her 18-year-old son for the last time.

Ricardo Martinez left home that day for a cattle ranch, tucked away in the Sierra Nevada mountains of northern Colombia, where he said he had been hired as a day labourer to help vaccinate a herd.

A week later, on the morning of September 21, police stormed the ranch, targeting a top commander of the Conquering Self-Defence Forces of the Sierra Nevada (ACSN), a paramilitary force that traffics cocaine to Central America, the United States and Europe.

President Abelardo de la Espriella appeared that night before the media, praising the operation that had ended in the deaths of seven alleged paramilitary fighters and three arrests.

"This is undoubtedly a major blow to this narcoterrorist organisation," he said.

Seven white body bags, laid out near a table full of semi-automatic rifles and ammunition, were presented as evidence of the operation's success. Inside one of the body bags was Martinez.

The raid was one of the most high-profile operations of de la Espriella's security crackdown since he took office in August. He has pledged to wage all-out war against Colombia's armed groups, abandoning the country's peace talks and prioritising military offensives instead.

His iron-fisted strategy, he says, will help to secure peace after more than six decades of internal armed conflict in Colombia.

But the operation, which killed Jose Perez, the ACSN's second-in-command, has prompted allegations that a civilian, Martinez, was killed and falsely presented as a paramilitary fighter.

"My son was not part of any armed group," said Rodriguez. "All I want is for justice to be served and my son's name to be cleared because he had nothing to do with the [ACSN]."

The case has ignited fears of a return to one of the darkest chapters in Colombia's internal conflict: a wave of extrajudicial killings known as the "false positives" scandal.

Between 1990 and 2016, state agents killed more than 7,800 civilians and presented them as enemy fighters, according to Colombia's Special Jurisdiction for Peace, a state tribunal.

"We fear that we could see a resurgence of false positives," said Lerber Dimas, the director of the Human Rights Defenders Platform of Sierra Nevada, an organisation that investigates human rights abuses.

Even politicians have warned of the possibility. Representative Daniel Monroy led a protest in Colombia's Congress to highlight Martinez's death, calling it the "first extrajudicial execution of the Abelardo de la Espriella administration".

"Why are they killing young people and presenting them as combat casualties?" the left-wing congressman asked.

Separately, Monroy posted on social media: "I never thought Abelardo would resort to the 'false positives' so soon."

articles.title: Tate Liverpool to reopen in autumn 2027
articles.summary: The gallery will relaunch after four years with an exhibition on surrealism.
articles.body:
Tate Liverpool is expected to reopen in autumn 2027 after a £30m transformation.

The gallery at Royal Albert Dock closed in October 2023 for a major redevelopment project. It had originally been due to reopen in 2025, but funding delays pushed back the timetable.

Tate Liverpool said its reopening programme would begin with a major surrealism exhibition featuring works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray.

The exhibition will echo the gallery's inaugural show in May 1988, when works from Tate's surrealist collection were the first to go on display at the venue.

Tate Liverpool said Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds would be the first exhibition to explore surrealism's relationship with the performing arts.

The show, which runs from autumn 2027 to spring 2028, will feature paintings, sculptures, costumes, masks and films from collections in the UK and abroad.

"Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool," said interim director Jemima Pyne.

She said the exhibition would "spark imaginations" and echo the surrealist show that opened the gallery in the 1980s.

The redevelopment of the Grade I listed warehouse, built in 1845, has been funded through a £10m government levelling-up grant, £6.6m from the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, £1.25m from the Wolfson Foundation and other donations.

Plans include a new ground-floor Art Hall, more flexible public spaces and panoramic views across the River Mersey.

Tate said the changes would allow the gallery to welcome up to one million visitors a year, five times the number it was originally designed to accommodate when it opened in 1988.

articles.title: A Florida couple signed a $2.775 million contract for a custom home and paid a $257,500 deposit, but construction never began; five years later, an appeals court reversed a $126,624.63 damages award
articles.summary: A Florida couple's legal battle over a failed $2.775 million custom home contract takes a turn as an appeals court reverses a damages award, ruling for arbitration instead. Discover the details behind the case and its implications.
articles.body: A Florida couple who paid $257,500 towards a $2.775 million custom home in Tampa, only for the construction project to collapse before work began, have seen a damages award of $126,624.63 reversed by an appeals court.The Sixth District Court of Appeal of Florida ruled on Wednesday that the couple's claims of fraudulent misrepresentation and violations of consumer protection law against the construction company's owners should have been referred to arbitration under the agreement they signed.The decision overturns the amended final judgment entered by an Orange County trial court against Susan Zimmerman and Tom Zimmerman, who owned Madison Construction. The case has been sent back for proceedings to enforce the contract's arbitration provision.The dispute began in 2020, when Carlos R. Diez-Arguelles and his wife, Maria Tejedor, approached Madison Construction to design and build a home on a waterfront property in Tampa.$257,500 home deposit became a legal battleThe couple first signed a design agreement with Madison in July 2020, paying a fee that would later be credited towards construction costs. They entered into a construction contract in November that year, setting the total project price at $2.775 million.The agreement required a non-refundable deposit of 10 per cent. After accounting for the design fee, the couple paid $257,500 on the day they signed the construction contract.Madison continued working on the project into mid-2021, with Tejedor exchanging emails about changes to the initial design. In July that year, Tom Zimmerman told the couple to expect updated plans, a revised payment schedule and new pricing through a DocuSign document.The couple disputed the changes and refused to sign the updated documents. Over the following two months, Diez-Arguelles sent letters demanding an account of the money paid and asking the company either to begin construction under the original agreement or return the deposit.Madison subsequently declared the couple in default and sent them a cheque for $150,875.37, representing the amount it calculated was refundable under the contract.The dispute later reached court. Diez-Arguelles alleged that the Zimmermans had misrepresented their professional qualifications, including claims that they were licensed contractors. He also alleged that they failed to disclose that Madison's licensed contractor, Garland Knight, would not personally supervise the project, and that the company's in-house design professional was not a licensed architect.The Zimmermans denied making the alleged misrepresentations.Why the appeals court overturned the damages awardThe Orange County trial court initially ruled in favour of Diez-Arguelles on his fraudulent misrepresentation claim. In an amended final judgment, it also found the Zimmermans liable under the Florida Deceptive and Unfair Trade Practices Act (FDUTPA) and awarded $126,624.63 in damages.The Zimmermans challenged the decision, arguing, among other things, that the construction contract required disputes to go through mediation and arbitration rather than court proceedings.The appeals court agreed that the trial court had wrongly rejected their request to enforce that provision.In its opinion, the panel noted that the contract covered disputes connected to the construction agreement, dealings between the owners and contractor, and alleged representations made by the contractor or its representatives.It also found that the Zimmermans, although not signatories to the agreement in their personal capacity, were Madison's agents and were entitled to enforce the arbitration clause as intended third-party beneficiaries.The judges said the couple's allegations were directly connected to the construction contract because they concerned the money paid towards the project, the company's failure to return the remaining deposit and representations made during the contractual relationship.The court therefore reversed the judgment against the Zimmermans on the fraud and FDUTPA claims and remanded the case for enforcement of the arbitration provision.The ruling did not establish that the alleged misrepresentations were false or that the Zimmermans were free from liability. Instead, it determined that the claims must be addressed through the agreed dispute-resolution process.The appeals court also upheld the trial court's decision finding Knight not liable on those claims. Its rulings in favour of all three defendants on the separate theft, statutory civil theft and conversion claims remained unchanged.The decision was issued by the Sixth District Court of Appeal on November 25, 2026, with Chief Judge Traver and Judge Brownlee concurring.You use AI every day. articles.title: Oscar-nominated Iranian screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian arrested in Tehran
articles.summary: Iranian rights activist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian has been arrested at his home in Tehran, a day after he warned that two
articles.body: Iranian rights activist and Oscar-nominated screenwriter Mehdi Mahmoudian has been arrested at his home in Tehran, a day after he warned that two protesters jailed over the 2022 anti-government demonstrations were at risk of execution.Mahmoudian was detained by security agents on Wednesday, who also seized his electronic devices, according to a post on his personal Telegram channel. A subsequent message said he had been charged with anti-government “propaganda” and “spreading false information”. He is being held at the Greater Tehran Penitentiary, according to his friend and Europe-based Iranian activist Hosein Razzagh, who spoke to The Associated Press (AP).Razzagh said he last spoke to Mahmoudian by phone at around 2-3 am on Wednesday, when they discussed a death penalty case linked to the 2022 protests. Mahmoudian later stopped answering his calls. Witnesses told Razzagh that more than a dozen armed agents had raided his home and taken him into custody. He also alleged that the screenwriter had been badly beaten while in detention.Mahmoudian's arrest came a day after he posted on Telegram that two protesters, Milad Armoun and Navid Najaran, faced the risk of execution within 24 hours. UN Special Rapporteur Mai Sato had also raised concerns about their cases, saying they were “scheduled to be executed at dawn tomorrow”. Mahmoudian later posted that, according to a lawyer and the families, the executions had not taken place.Razzagh said Mahmoudian had openly campaigned on behalf of jailed protesters and those facing execution, adding that Iranian authorities “are extremely sensitive about execution cases”.Mahmoudian co-wrote the Iranian film It Was Just an Accident, directed by Jafar Panahi. The film was nominated for the Academy Award for best international feature film, bringing international attention to the screenwriter and his work.Mahmoudian had also been arrested in February, shortly before the Academy Awards, after signing a statement with 16 others condemning Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and the government's violent crackdown on demonstrators following mass anti-government protests in January.Mahmoudian's activism has centred on people detained during Iran's protest movements. The 2022 demonstrations erupted after the death of 22-year-old Mahsa Amini, who was arrested by Iran's morality police over allegations that she had not worn her headscarf properly.The protests triggered a months-long crackdown in which hundreds of people were killed and thousands detained. The Oslo-based Iran Human Rights group has reported that at least 15 protesters have been executed in connection with the demonstrations, including two in 2026.Iranian authorities have continued to arrest people linked to the January protests and stepped up executions of jailed demonstrators. articles.title: Spain’s far right hasn’t governed since Franco. Immigration fears could change that.
articles.summary: The campaign hymn blared through the meeting hall in Badalona, a working-class city on Barcelona’s northern flank with a large immigrant population.
articles.body: BARCELONA, Spain — The campaign hymn blared through the meeting hall in Badalona, a working-class city on Barcelona’s northern flank with a large immigrant population. Its lyrics set the tone for the rally of Spain’s far-right party. Passionately sung by a husky baritone, the song “National Priority” depicts common Spaniards barely holding their own in a warlike struggle for their country — before the messianic cavalry arrives in the form of the Vox party and its bearded, barrel-chested leader, Santiago Abascal. It reflects one of Vox’s key policy pledges: if empowered after Sunday’s national election, the government will start prioritizing the needs of Spanish citizens over foreign residents and immigrants. Its other big pledge echoes what has already been put into effect in the U.S.: the expulsion of migrants. The message resonated with attendees, who waved Spanish red-and-yellow and Vox’s green flags. Pablo Guerrero, a 43-year-old and father of six who works in sales, said he was drawn to Vox for its unabashed defense of Spain’s Catholic roots. A young man applauding enthusiastically wore a soccer jersey of Spain’s star player, Lamine Yamal, himself a first-generation Spaniard born to immigrants from Africa. “I started by getting past all the taboos that people associated with Vox,” Carla Sabater, a 25-year-old law student, told The Associated Press. “And when I really saw what its leaders were saying, I saw it was just like any other party to vote for, but one that could bring real change.” For decades since the repression of Francisco Franco’s 20th-century dictatorship, Spaniards convinced of liberal democracy’s benefits have kept far-right parties from government. But in recent years, anti-immigration populism across Europe and the U.S. has presented an alternative that started appealing to some in Spain, which has seen surges of migrants this year as the government granted amnesty to 1 million undocumented people. That leaves Vox with an opportunity to grab its share of power, shifting Spain’s political paradigm. Vox moves into mainstream Like Marine Le Pen’s National Rally that is aiming to take power in France’s election next year, Vox has transformed from a group with fringe appeal to garnering broader support over the past decade. The coming year will also feature elections in Italy, Greece and Poland. Vox is banking on its hardline immigration stance to win over voters and enable it to play kingmaker for Spain’s traditional Popular Party conservatives. In exchange for backing PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo as Spain’s next prime minister, Vox would join a coalition government and push for a crackdown on migrants. A PP-Vox government would “mean another step in the normalization of the far right across Europe,” Steven Forti, professor of political science at the Autonomous University of Barcelona, told the AP. In Spain’s 2023 election, incumbent Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez warned that Vox could enter government with the PP as a means to rally broad support. His playbook this time is similar. “A government of the PP that includes Vox would not be just another government; it would mean an enormous step backwards. It would mean rolling back the clock 40, 50 years,” Sánchez said in a recent interview with El País. The comment was a barely veiled reference to the last time an ultranationalist party was in power. Under Franco, political rivals were executed and persecuted, elections were eliminated and an almost theocratic conservative Catholic regime was enforced. But bandying about Franco’s ghost holds ever less sway for younger voters, many of whom have only the faintest idea of life under that repressive regime, said political analyst Montserrat Nebrera, a former senior member of the PP in Catalonia. “People have lost their fear of what Vox is capable of and, despite its proposals, they think it will stay within the bounds of the traditional democratic state,” Nebrera told the AP. “Whether that will prove to be true is another matter. But that is the idea that is percolating among voters: that it is not a big deal after all.” Abascal has rejected the label “far right,” saying that the term is meant to denigrate Vox as well as the parties of Le Pen or Viktor Orbán in Hungary. He calls Vox’s positions those of “common sense.” But political scientists agree that its policies put it to the right of traditional right-wing parties on the political spectrum, for example, in Vox’s refusal to support laws to protect women from gender violence. And while Abascal himself came from the PP, some other high-ranking Vox members came from the pro-Franco Falange party. Spain’s porous borders Sánchez is virtually alone among European leaders in defending migration as a means to grow the economy while culturally enriching the nation and upholding universal human rights. Last week five European countries, including center-right Germany and the Socialist-led Denmark, announced an agreement to send migrants to Rwanda. Vox has pounced on migratory crises afflicting Spain’s borders. Abascal has called the crossing of tens of thousands of mostly young Moroccans into Spain’s north African exclave of Ceuta in July an “invasion.” He kicked off his campaign in the Canary Islands, which have seen a surge in arrivals of people, mostly from Senegal, by boat this month. While Spain’s business community and Catholic bishops backed Sánchez’s amnesty program, Abascal slammed it as encouraging more people to come. Some voters saw the subsequent surges of migrants to Ceuta and the Canary Islands as validation of his claim. At the rally, the public had turned out to hear Vox’s new star and ideologue, Carlos Hernández Quero. The young historian breaks with Vox’s tailored, macho aesthetic: he is skinny and sports an earring and a scruffy beard and hairdo. He spent half an hour arguing that the arrival of millions of migrants has harmed the job prospects of Spain’s working class, soaking up welfare benefits and driving up demand for housing. “The Left has become public enemy number one because it has destroyed public services that are supposed to help those who most need them. It has all been ruined,” Hernández Quero said. “And that is because immigration has undermined our welfare system.” Sánchez is counting on worries over housing costs to override immigration concerns at the ballot box. He has also warned that Vox will take aim at progressive abortion and euthanasia laws as well as green energy policies. David Paredes, a member of Sánchez’s Socialist party, told the AP that “people aren’t talking about immigration” when he canvassed for votes in Barcelona. He said they appreciate that foreigners help fill jobs in healthcare and sectors like construction that benefit everyone. Spain’s leader since 2018, Sánchez boasts that he has overseen Europe’s fastest growing economy while increasing the minimum wage. But many voters haven’t felt the benefits amid a cost-of-living crunch, and some seem willing to give Vox a shot. “We must put people from here first, before people who come from elsewhere,” said Jenny Rodríguez, a 34-year-old shop clerk attending the rally. “And then we want immigration to be brought under control.”

articles.title: UK antisemitism advisor launches probe into BBC, says culture demands Jewish staffers 'justify' existence
articles.summary: The United Kingdom's antisemitism advisor, Lord John Mann, is investigating the BBC, citing accounts from current and former Jewish employees.
articles.body: The United Kingdom's independent advisor on antisemitism announced Thursday that the BBC will be investigated over antisemitism concerns, according to reports. Lord John Mann wrote to the BBC informing them of his investigation. "I am a big supporter of the BBC and public broadcasting. It is precisely because I believe in the future of the BBC that I need to intervene now and in this way," Mann said in an announcement about the inquiry, according to Variety. JEWISH EDUCATORS FACE RAMPANT ANTISEMITISM IN TEACHERS UNIONS, NEW REPORT FINDS Mann said in his announcement that his investigation came based on what he has heard from current and former Jewish BBC employees. "The personal validations that I hear from former and current BBC Jewish employees and contractors is that fundamentally there is an institutional culture that demands that Jewish people must be expected to justify their existence, their identity, how they define their Jewishness," he said, according to Variety. ANTISEMITISM FEARS PUSH JEWISH MED SCHOOL STUDENTS, PROVIDERS AND PATIENTS TO HIDE FAITH, ADL FINDS Mann named multiple reporters, including Jeremy Bowen, John Simpson, Feargal Keeane and Kate Adie, Variety reported. He continued, "I defend their right to report. I am for free speech, not restrictions on speech. Including, by the way, when academics or others say things that I fundamentally disagree with." Mann said institutions that stifle Jewish perspectives are the "antithesis of free speech or fair and honest broadcasting." He noted he would speak to every Jewish employee at the BBC as part of his investigation. EXCLUSIVE: JEWISH PHYSICIAN WINS RELIGIOUS EXEMPTION FROM UNION MEMBERSHIP AND FEES OVER ISRAEL STANCES "We take any and all allegations of discrimination extremely seriously – there is no place for it at the BBC. We have introduced compulsory training on antisemitism for all our staff and we actively encourage colleagues to report any incidences or concerns they have," a BBC spokesperson told Fox News Digital in a statement. "We are determined to ensure the BBC is a place where everyone can be themselves and feel accepted." BBC producer Lucie Kon said in October, according to a report from the BBC, that she was given a £400,000 payout after raising antisemitism concerns at the broadcasting company. Kon's position was eliminated during a company restructure, the BBC reported. TRUMP WINS PERMISSION TO FILE AMENDED COMPLAINT IN $10B DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AGAINST BBC She said the "payment was for redundancy back pay and settlement for personal injury caused by the process," the report read. President Donald Trump filed a $10 billion lawsuit against the BBC late last year for its 2024 "Panorama" documentary that allegedly distorted his remarks to supporters on Jan. 6, 2021. A judge ruled on Nov. 10 that the defamation lawsuit can proceed. "A Huge Victory against Fake News BBC, a terrible abuser of the truth, just handed down by highly respected District Court Judge, Jeffrey T. Kuntz, of the Southern District of Florida," Trump wrote on Truth Social. BBC CALLS FRANCE PROTESTS 'MOSTLY PEACEFUL' AS FOOTAGE SHOWS RIOTERS TORCHING CARS, BATTLING POLICE CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE In his ruling, Kuntz criticized the BBC over how it edited the 2024 "Panorama" documentary at the center of the lawsuit, suggesting the broadcaster "knew or should have known that the segment they were creating would not and could not have been a truthful statement." articles.title: Huntingdon train knifeman guilty of trying to murder 14 people
articles.summary: Anthony Williams, 33, is convicted of 10 attacks on a train and four in Peterborough and London.
articles.body:
A knifeman has been found guilty of attempting to murder 14 people, including 10 on board a train to London.

Passengers on the Doncaster to King's Cross service fought off Anthony Williams, 33, with a frying pan and a toaster as the attack unfolded on 1 November 2025.

Some hid in toilets and bike racks before the driver was forced to make an unscheduled stop in Huntingdon, Cambridgeshire, where Williams was arrested by armed police.

As well as the train attacks, Williams, of Langford Road, Peterborough, was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Jurors deliberated for 15 hours and 53 minutes before delivering seven guilty verdicts, and then returned an hour later to give the final seven.

The judge, Mr Justice Calver KC, said the victims handled themselves with "great dignity throughout" the trial.

Aside from the attack on the LNER train, Williams also attempted to murder a boy and two men in Peterborough on 31 October 2025, and then a teenager on a DLR train in east London hours later.

The defendant, who appeared at court via a video link from a secure hospital, showed little emotion as each verdict was delivered.

Reacting to the verdicts, Ben Samples, of the Crown Prosecution Service, said: "The fact that nobody was killed in his rampage is down to the courage, quick thinking and good fortune of the people he attacked."

It has now emerged that in the month before the attacks, Williams twice contacted his GP to say the anti-psychosis drugs he was taking for schizophrenia were not working.

A spokesperson for NHS East of England said it would be investigating the care provided to Williams.

Cambridgeshire Police has also apologised for missed opportunities "that may have prevented" the stabbings.

Assistant Chief Constable Leighton Hammett said an alleged assault in Peterborough on 27 September 2025, several weeks before the train attacks, had been linked to Williams.

Darryl Preston, police and crime commissioner for Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, said two officers faced misconduct proceedings over their handling of the incident and the investigation remained ongoing.

How the Huntingdon train attack unfolded - carriage by carriage

Williams's knife attack on the LNER service began when he stabbed Jonathan Gjoshe – then a Scunthorpe United footballer – at 19:37 GMT.

The defender later informed police his whole arm was "drenched with blood".

Other victims included Scott Bletcher, stabbed six times in his seat as he returned from a Christmas shopping trip.

Bletcher told jurors he thought, "This is what it feels like to die" after being knifed.

The court also heard from Nottingham Forest football fan Stephen Crean, who decided "he had to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

CCTV footage played to the jury showed LNER staff member Samir Zitouni use a frying pan to fend off Williams.

He said to the knifeman "we love you, we can help you" as he thought it was "better than swearing at him".

After the train stopped, Zitouni fell between the train and the platform. His lungs were punctured and he needed four blood transfusions, chest drains and the assistance of a ventilator.

Having been arrested in Huntingdon railway station's car park, Williams was said to be "acting strangely" and "completely unfazed by what had occurred... he was rocking and laughing".

If you've been a victim of crime, details of help and support are available at BBC Action Line .

One police officer noted he "appeared to be talking to himself" and spoke about the devil.

Consultant forensic psychiatrist Dr Bernard Chin told the trial Williams, who did not give evidence in his defence, was "suffering from an acute relapse of schizophrenia" at the time of the attacks.

Jurors heard Williams had "the delusional premise that his life was at risk by a wide-ranging conspiracy by the devil".

As well as Gjoshe, Bletcher, Crean, and Zitouni, Williams was also convicted of attempting to murder Raza Aslam, Sachin Balakrishnan, Kevin Deely, Scott Green, Michael Paffett and David Presland on the train.

Williams also attempted to murder Dawid Taborski, William Ogelby and a 14-year-old boy, who cannot be identified, in Peterborough the night before.

The boy, who was about to go trick or treating with a friend, told police: "This random guy… he just pulled out a knife and stabbed me."

He said it "didn't feel like [Williams] was mentally sane. His eyes were wide open, like he was on something."

After those attacks, Williams boarded a London-bound train where he was heard saying: "I am the baddest, no-one is as bad as me".

A passenger texted British Transport Police (BTP) reporting a male behaving erratically, but the man dropped down on to the tracks at Stevenage and police officers deemed it unsafe to pursue him.

Then, in the early hours of 1 November, Williams sliced the face of teenager Isaiah Idris on a DLR train in east London with a knife.

Idris described how his attacker had repeatedly asked: "Are you beefing the devil?"

Det Supt Sam Blackburn, from BTP, said Williams' offending had sparked "one of the most significant and complex" investigations in the force's history.

"The events that unfolded onboard the train on 1 November were unlike anything previously encountered before, and Anthony Williams created what I can only describe as a terrifying scene of fear and violence."

articles.title: Second court defeat for Trump's deep-sea mining ambitions
articles.summary: Second judge rules against Trump administration's plans to lease areas of ocean floor and survey for mining.
articles.body:
The Trump administration's plans to begin deep-sea mining in the Pacific have hit a second legal setback after a federal judge ruled plans to lease areas of sea-floor off the Northern Mariana Islands violated the Endangered Species Act (ESA).

The court's decision follows a similar ruling over a proposed lease sale off American Samoa.

Opposition groups who lodged the Northern Mariana Islands lawsuit said they were concerned deep-sea mining could cause long-term damage to the ocean ecosystem.

The US government has said it wants to start deep-sea mining to enable access to critical minerals and to counter China's growing influence over crucial components needed for electronics.

The administration had planned to put up for sale leases for the Northern Mariana Islands on 16 December 2026.

It is not clear what will happen next as the administration chose not to recognise the first court ruling and went ahead with the sale of two leases covering 13 million hectares (more than 30 million acres) off American Samoa.

Opponents have vowed to challenge that sale.

Ruling on the Northern Mariana Islands case, District judge Jill Aiko Otake said the defendants, the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS), which provided the expert opinion behind the lease sales, and Howard Lutnick, who was named in his capacity as head of the department that oversees the agency, had failed to consider the potential effects that could follow once the leases were issued.

The ruling explained that while these leases would only authorise the leaseholder to conduct preliminary surveying activity, they might eventually allow the leaseholder to actually mine the ocean's floor.

The potential impact of that mining had not been addressed in the biodiversity assessment which was used to sign off the lease sales, the ruling said.

Using machines to mine for minerals in the deep ocean is highly controversial.

Some scientists have raised concerns that deep-sea mining could damage little-understood deep-ocean ecosystems, though industry supporters argue the environmental effects remain uncertain and require further study.

Deep-sea mining uses vacuum technology to suck up nodules from the muddy sediment. However, this process also removes organisms that grow on them, including corals and sponges, many of which cannot grow anywhere else.

In one study of the impact of deep-sea mining, researchers found more than 4,000 animals, 90% of which were new species, living on the seafloor in a remote area of the Pacific Ocean.

Some critics of the industry fear that before we have the chance to explore the full nature of life in the undiscovered deep ocean, it could be endangered.

Norway was the first country in the world to approve commercial-scale deep-sea mining in 2024 .

Over 2,000 of the world's scientists met in 2025 to review the data on ocean health and they recommended governments halt deep sea exploration while further research on the impacts was carried out.

More than 30 countries supported this position and called for a moratorium.

Shortly before that meeting, President Trump published executive orders to push ahead with mining and "unleash America's offshore critical minerals and resources".

He said "these resources are key to strengthening our economy, securing our energy future, and reducing dependence on foreign suppliers for critical minerals".

Part of the plan aims to "counter China's growing influence over seabed mineral resources".

Deep-sea mining targets polymetallic nodules – potato-sized rocks found over 4,000 metres below the ocean surface.

These contain minerals including nickel, cobalt, and manganese which are used in manufactruring electronics and batteries.

They are also important for renewable energy technologies to tackle climate change, including solar panels, wind turbines and electric vehicles.

The International Energy Agency predicts that demand for the minerals could at least double by 2040.

U.S. Department of Commerce‘s The National Marine Fisheries Service refused to comment.

articles.title: US customs open a parcel from UAE headed to an Illinois home and find 440 fake Cartier, Tiffany and Bulgari jewellery pieces with a potential retail value of $2.4 million
articles.summary: A parcel travelling from the United Arab Emirates to a residential address in Illinois took an unexpected turn when US customs officers selected it for
articles.body: A parcel travelling from the United Arab Emirates to a residential address in Illinois took an unexpected turn when US customs officers selected it for inspection. Inside were hundreds of jewellery pieces carrying the names of some of the world's best-known luxury houses, including Cartier, Tiffany & Co., Chanel and Bulgari. The collection appeared to represent a shipment worth millions of dollars at retail prices. But there was a significant difference between what the labels suggested and what the items actually were. An examination by US Customs and Border Protection (CBP) specialists established that all 440 pieces were counterfeit. The shipment was seized before reaching its intended destination.US customs seize 440 counterfeit luxury jewellery pieces in $2.4 million shipmentThe pieces were identified on November 11, 2026, when CBP officers working at the Cincinnati port examined a shipment originating in the UAE. Although the parcel was addressed to a private residence in Illinois, it was selected for further inspection before it could continue through the import process.Officers found 440 jewellery items carrying trademarks associated with seven luxury brands. These included Cartier, Tiffany, Chanel, Christian Dior, Van Cleef & Arpels, Bvlgari and Hermes. The collection contained products bearing the branding of companies whose jewellery and accessories are sold in markets around the world.The items were subsequently examined by CBP's Centers of Excellence and Expertise, which employ specialists familiar with different industries and their products. Their assessment established that the pieces were not genuine merchandise. Customs officials seized the entire shipment because the goods carried counterfeit versions of registered and recorded trademarks.Fake luxury jewellery shipment had a potential retail value of $2.4 millionThe estimated value attached to the shipment was based on what the jewellery would have cost had the pieces been authentic. According to CBP, the combined manufacturer's suggested retail price would have exceeded $2.4 million.Note: The figure does not represent the actual value of the counterfeit goods or money recovered from the shipment. Rather, it reflects the potential retail value of genuine products bearing the same brand identities.The difference matters because counterfeit merchandise can use familiar luxury names and trademarks without having any legitimate connection to the companies that own them. In this case, the presence of several major jewellery and fashion labels in one parcel prompted an assessment involving the agency's specialist teams.CBP announced the seizure on November 18, releasing details of the inspection a week after the shipment was intercepted.Why US customs can seize counterfeit branded merchandiseThe seizure falls within CBP's wider responsibility for enforcing intellectual property protections at the US border. The agency can detain imported goods, seize them and pursue their forfeiture and destruction when they violate applicable trademark or copyright protections.For a trademark to qualify for this particular enforcement process, it must be registered with the United States Patent and Trademark Office and recorded with CBP. The system allows customs officers to identify protected brand names and take action when imported merchandise appears to infringe those rights.Counterfeit products are not limited to jewellery. Customs officials regularly deal with imitation clothing, handbags, electronics and other consumer goods that use branding without authorisation. Other import violations can involve incorrect product classifications, misleading country-of-origin information, inaccurate valuations or goods that fail to meet health and safety requirements.Cincinnati Port Director Eric Zizelman said, “Counterfeit goods are poor quality products that cost the U.S. businesses billions of dollars a year while robbing our country of jobs and tax revenues.”“CBP remains committed to stopping counterfeit smuggling, taking profits from organized crime, and helping protect our communities from potentially hazardous knockoffs.”CBP warns consumers about signs of counterfeit productsAccording to CBP, consumers can take the following precautions when purchasing branded goods:Check product quality: Look for poor stitching, uneven finishes, peeling labels and other signs of substandard manufacturing.Inspect the packaging: Low-quality printing, spelling mistakes and inferior packaging may indicate counterfeit merchandise.Verify the product: Check whether the item actually exists in the brand's official collection.Watch for faulty electronics: Counterfeit devices may have unusually short battery life or overheat during normal use.Buy from authorised sellers: Purchase directly from the brand owner or its authorised retailers whenever possible.Check online sellers: Read customer reviews and verify whether the seller provides a working US telephone number and a valid contact address.Consult CBP guidance: Refer to the agency's E-Commerce Counterfeit Awareness Guide before making online purchases.You use AI every day. articles.title: Psychiatric care under scrutiny after abuse scandals in Croatia and Bosnia
articles.summary: Persistent failures in psychiatric care have been exposed, including staff shortages, poor training and weak oversight.
articles.body:
Thousands gathered in Zagreb’s Ban Josip Jelacic Square on Saturday, carrying white pillows marked with bloody handprints.

The symbolic protest was held in memory of 32-year-old Kristian Josip Peris, who died at the Sveti Ivan Psychiatric Clinic in the Croatian capital after medical staff allegedly tried to restrain him by placing a pillow over his face, according to publicly released security camera footage.

Several days later, footage from the psychiatric ward of a public hospital in the city of Zenica, in neighbouring Bosnia and Herzegovina, sparked public outrage. The video showed medical staff physically assaulting a patient.

The two cases in neighbouring countries led to the arrest of at least 13 healthcare workers, the resignations of the heads of the psychiatric institutions involved, and a wave of public anger.

But they also raised a broader question: What happens behind the closed doors of institutions meant to protect some of society’s most vulnerable people?

These are not the first cases to have shocked the region.

Bosnia and Herzegovina still remembers the Pazaric institutional abuse scandal, involving a small settlement located about 30km (18.6 miles) from the capital, Sarajevo, where residents of a state institution for children and young people with additional needs were tied to radiators and subjected to physical abuse.

Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, once part of the same country, Yugoslavia, have spent the past three decades trying to bring their healthcare systems and societies closer to European standards.

Croatia joined the European Union in 2013, while Bosnia and Herzegovina is forging its own path towards membership.

Unlike in some Western countries, where private healthcare providers play a significant role in mental health services, psychiatric inpatient care in Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia is predominantly provided through public healthcare institutions.

Although private providers also operate in the region, public institutions remain central to the provision of specialised psychiatric hospital care.

This makes the role of public authorities particularly important, not only in ensuring access to treatment but also in supervising institutions, maintaining adequate staffing levels and protecting patients’ rights.

‘Problem lies in consistently following those protocols’

Edin Bjelosevic, a neuropsychiatrist and university professor from Zenica, said the legal frameworks in countries that emerged from the breakup of Yugoslavia largely reflect contemporary standards for treating people with mental health conditions.

“The problem lies in consistently following those protocols, rather than in access to modern treatments and procedures,” Bjelosevic told Al Jazeera.

According to Eurostat, the EU’s statistical office, about 96,000 psychiatrists were working across 25 member countries in 2024. Germany had the highest number relative to its population, with 29 psychiatrists per 100,000 people. Croatia recorded 19.1, above the European average, while Serbia had 12.4 psychiatrists per 100,000 people.

Bosnia and Herzegovina, according to World Health Organization (WHO) data from 2020, had just 9.48 psychiatrists per 100,000 people. More recent comparable figures for the country are not available.

Differences are also evident in the number of psychiatric hospital beds. Croatia had 93 beds per 100,000 people, compared with the European average of 71. Serbia recorded 82, while Bosnia and Herzegovina, with 40 beds per 100,000 people, was significantly below the average.

Eurostat and WHO figures may differ from data published by national statistical agencies.

However, the number of psychiatrists and hospital beds alone does not provide a complete picture of the quality of care, patient safety or the working conditions of healthcare professionals.

In its 2024-2025 report, Croatia’s Ombudswoman called on the Ministry of Health to improve the functioning of psychiatric institutions. Among the recommendations was better training for medical staff in the use of coercive measures involving people with mental health conditions.

Coercive measures are used in psychiatric institutions around the world. They involve temporarily restricting a patient’s freedom of movement to prevent an immediate risk of harm to themselves or others. However, they are not intended as a routine means of controlling patients, but as a last resort when other approaches have failed.

Following Peris’s death, Croatia’s Ministry of Health identified shortcomings at the clinic, ordering five corrective measures.

The inspection found faults in staff training and staffing levels, alongside problems with the supervision of patients subjected to coercive measures, medical record-keeping and reporting procedures following the patient’s death.

Staffing levels did not meet the required standards, with a shortage of one physiotherapist and one nursing assistant. The ministry also found faults in the scope and quality of staff training on managing patients in crisis situations.

Health Minister Irena Hrstic said four of the five corrective measures were to take effect immediately, while the clinic was given 60 days to bring its staffing levels into line with the required standards.

The findings highlighted concerns that go beyond the conduct of individual healthcare workers, raising questions about staffing, training and institutional oversight in psychiatric care.

Abdulah Kucukalic, a neuropsychiatrist from Sarajevo, said psychiatric institutions across the region share a common problem: a shortage of non-medical personnel specifically trained to deal safely with patients experiencing acute psychiatric crises.

“I think the legislation is in line with, or very close to, international standards. Our doctors are also frequently cited in international professional circles. But our psychiatric institutions lack non-medical staff trained to manage patients safely,” Kucukalic told Al Jazeera.

He warned that situations are particularly risky when patients in severe acute conditions arrive at hospitals in the late afternoon or at night, when staffing levels are significantly lower.

“My experience is that patients in acute conditions arrive in the afternoon or at night, in extremely serious states. At that point, you may have just one doctor and two healthcare workers in the hospital. They are not in a position to manage such a patient safely,” Kucukalic said.

The cases in Zagreb and Zenica illustrate how thin the line can be between providing care and putting at risk the very people who need protection most.

articles.title: Judge strikes down Trump’s latest restrictions on US birthright citizenship
articles.summary: After a Supreme Court ruling against it, the Trump administration had tried a narrower set of restrictions.
articles.body:
A United States federal judge has blocked an attempt by President Donald Trump’s administration to deny birthright citizenship to certain categories of US-born children whose parents it argued were not subject to US jurisdiction.

In a ruling issued on Wednesday, District Court Judge Christopher Cooper said those children were still under US jurisdiction and thus were guaranteed citizenship under the US Constitution.

“The president cannot carve out new exceptions to birthright citizenship for children born within the United States and subject to its laws,” Cooper said in the order.

Another court in Maryland had also blocked the same policy by the Trump administration in a September ruling, issuing a preliminary injunction at the time.

The new ruling is another blow to Trump’s campaign to end birthright citizenship for children whose parents were not American citizens or legal permanent residents at their birth.

The Trump administration has argued that the US Constitution’s 14th Amendment – which says all “persons born or naturalised in the United States, and subject to the jurisdiction thereof, are citizens of the United States” – was not meant to apply to parents who were not permanently living in the country.

The latest lawsuit was brought by several rights groups on behalf of children who would be affected by Trump’s executive orders in August that targeted birthright citizenship.

The case was heard after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s initial order on birthright citizenship in June, ruling that the lawmakers who drafted the 14th Amendment knew how broad its language was and did not limit it in the way the president was trying to.

Trump, who had taken the rare step of personally attending arguments at the Supreme Court in that case, has said he is unhappy with the June ruling.

In it, the Supreme Court cited a previous case it had considered in 1898 brought by a US-born Chinese American who was being denied citizenship. Wong Kim Ark’s parents had left the US for their native China after he was born, and when Wong returned as an adult, he was denied entry with officials saying he was not considered a citizen.

Soon after the Supreme Court’s ruling, Trump tried to again restrict birthright citizenship with a new order taking aim at “birth tourism”, in which women travel ⁠to the US to give birth so their children can obtain automatic ⁠citizenship. The order also targeted children whose parents work for foreign governments or international organizations but lack diplomatic immunity and those who have a parent who is classified as an “alien enemy”.

The president “needs to accept that birthright citizenship is the law of the land”, said Cody Wofsy, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union, one of the groups representing plaintiffs in the latest case. “The Supreme Court has twice rejected efforts to gut birthright citizenship, in 1898 and again earlier this year. Third time is not the charm.”

White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said in a statement that the court’s decision was “just another ruling from an activist judge” and Trump’s order had been “consistent with the holdings and analysis set forth by the Supreme Court”.

In a study last year, the Migration Policy Institute estimated that about 255,000 babies a year who were born to parents who were unauthorised immigrants or on temporary visas and thus subject to Trump’s initial executive order would be denied citizenship if the Supreme Court had upheld that policy.

The 14th Amendment, ratified in 1868 after the US Civil War, automatically made those born to previously enslaved people citizens of the country. Its broad language, though, also extended to others born in the country, an interpretation US courts have said was in line with English traditions preceding the founding of the United States.

Indigenous people were seen as an exception to that provision because they enjoyed some legal autonomy, and it was not until 1924 that the US Congress passed a law granting them citizenship.

Since taking office, Trump has set out a broad agenda to restrict immigration, restricting visas and political asylum for much of the world and directing federal law enforcement agencies to institute a national crackdown on allegedly undocumented immigrants .

Along with trying to restrict who is granted birthright citizenship, the Trump administration has also stepped up lawsuits to strip already naturalised people of their status if they committed major crimes and concealed that history from authorities.

articles.title: Why are winter rains forcing Palestinians in Gaza to flee again?
articles.summary: Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians vulnerable.
articles.body:
When heavy rain swept through az-Zawayda in central Gaza in early November, water rushed into Jaber al-Kaseeh’s tent, soaking his family’s mattresses and spoiling their food.

Al-Kaseeh, who fled Beit Lahiya in northern Gaza, told Al Jazeera that his camp had flooded three or four times the previous winter. Those floods had already driven many of his neighbours away.

About 1.36 million Palestinians, 65 percent of Gaza’s population, are living in tents and makeshift shelters, according to the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

The storm that began on the evening of November 6 flooded about 70,000 tents within 12 hours, according to Gaza’s Government Media Office. Preliminary UN estimates suggest it affected about 226,000 people, including more than 5,000 households left sleeping without shelter. About 600 households were forced to move again.

The rain also killed people. On November 8, a sand embankment collapsed onto tents at a displacement camp south of Deir el-Balah, killing five people, including children. OCHA reported that an infant drowned during the same storm and a nine-month-old baby died of hypothermia on November 13.

The Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities warned on Wednesday that about 1,000 camps and other shelter sites could flood this winter. The councils say 200,000 worn-out tents need replacing and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse.

As Gaza enters its fourth winter since Israel launched its genocidal war in October 2023, we look at how Israeli restrictions on humanitarian aid, damaged buildings and flooded tents leave displaced Palestinians at greater risk.

Why can’t Palestinians move somewhere safer?

Israeli restrictions keep Palestinians from reaching large parts of Gaza, which leaves them fewer options to move to safer areas, according to OCHA. On November 17, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the World Food Programme said Gaza’s population had been confined to less than 40 percent of the territory and that more than half of its 1,700 displacement sites were on flood-prone land.

The threat of further displacement persists. On Thursday, Israel Katz, the defence minister in Israel’s caretaker government, threatened a new offensive that would move one million Palestinians south if Hamas did not disarm. Writing on X, he called Hamas’s control over the remaining 30 percent of Gaza “ an illusion ”. He did not issue an evacuation order.

Damaged homes offer little refuge. About 82 percent of Gaza’s structures had been damaged or destroyed by mid-June, according to UN satellite analysis.

In Nuseirat, Nasser al-Hajj took his children to a neighbour’s home during the first November storm as debris fell from the ceiling of his flat, which an Israeli attack had damaged. “But where am I supposed to go? Rent is expensive, and a tent is not safe either,” he told Al Jazeera .

Israel’s war has wrecked the drains and sewers that would normally carry rainwater away. In Gaza City, eight pumping stations and three main rainwater collection basins were out of service when the first storm hit, municipal spokesperson Hosni Muhanna said . Even under the best conditions, he said, the remaining network could handle no more than a fifth of the rainwater.

At Sheikh Radwan lagoon, one of the city’s main collection basins, the water rose by nearly 1.5 metres (five feet) during the storm, OCHA reported. Its pumping station is operating at less than 40 percent of its design capacity, the UN office added on Thursday.

In central Gaza, the councils are worried about water rising suddenly in Wadi Gaza and flooding al-Mughraqa and az-Zahra. Emergency services are overstretched: Gaza’s civil defence said it received 2,166 distress calls on November 7 but could send crews to only 218; most callers received advice by phone.

During the early November rains, the UN said crews used suction trucks to remove water mixed with sewage from 58 shelters. At the Patient’s Friends Benevolent Society Hospital in Gaza City, water flooded the basement that housed the children’s department, pharmacy and radiology services. Elsewhere, flooded roads kept patients and staff from reaching clinics.

Crowding poses a separate risk. Families in crowded tents have too little water to maintain basic hygiene, paediatrician Sharif Matar told Al Jazeera at Gaza City’s Rantisi Children’s Hospital.

The World Health Organization (WHO) recorded 692 suspected meningitis cases between October 1 and November 23, most of them among babies under a year old. Gaza’s Ministry of Health issued an epidemic alert on November 24 after recording 272 cases in October, compared with a usual monthly average of 30 to 50.

Why isn’t enough shelter aid reaching families?

On November 13, the UN’s humanitarian team said more than 150,000 tents bought by aid organisations and governments were waiting outside Gaza, most of them in Egypt’s El Arish. On Wednesday, the European Commission said tents were still waiting on trucks because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter. Goods from Egypt are routed for inspection through the Karem Abu Salem crossing (called Kerem Shalom in Israel) rather than entering directly through Rafah. Israeli authorities also classify some shelter supplies as “dual-use”, which limits how much aid groups can bring in.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said on Monday that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza under its winter programme. It said it had approved more than 67,000 tents and other winter supplies that had yet to be brought in. Inside Gaza, shelter agencies have fewer than 6,500 tents in stock, the Norwegian Refugee Council (NRC) said on Wednesday.

Restrictions and shortages have pushed up prices. Basic winter supplies for a family of six can cost more than $6,000 inside Gaza, compared with about $700 when aid agencies buy them abroad and bring them in, the NRC said. Donors have funded only 35 percent of the $283m needed for the minimum winter shelter response.

A tent crossing the border tells a family little about when help will reach its camp. In al-Mawasi, near Khan Younis, Fadi Wafi told the Palestinian news agency Wafa on Wednesday that his name had been put on a list of people affected by the last storm, but he had received no shelter supplies. His family of five had two mattresses and two blankets.

Gaza’s Government Media Office warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days. Aid workers have cleared drains, reinforced shelters and put up flood barriers, but OCHA reported on November 20 that such work had been recorded at only 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations that teams were tracking.

On Monday, IOM said Israeli authorities had approved about 70,000 pieces of timber and more than 1,200 toolkits to build sturdier emergency shelters for about 1,200 families. COGAT also said it had approved pumps and generators and would allow partial repairs at the Sheikh Ijlin and Sheikh Radwan sewage facilities. It did not say the equipment had arrived. COGAT has said reconstruction equipment will enter only after Hamas has fully disarmed. Gaza’s municipalities are still asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel.

For Om Hani Hamouda, whose family has been displaced about 15 times, the question is what they can live in when it rains again. “We want these tents to be replaced with caravans,” she told Al Jazeera after her tent flooded in az-Zawayda. “Even a simple caravan would be better.”

articles.title: EPA reports 'zero detection of airborne lead' day after Iowa lead azide detonation
articles.summary: The EPA reports zero detection of airborne lead after the detonation of five tons of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, Iowa.
articles.body: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) said Thursday that its air monitors continue to report "zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region" after the detonation of a stockpile of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant. The statement comes as the EPA said it collected more than 1,000 samples following Wednesday's controlled detonation of the bomb-making chemical in Middletown, Iowa. Nearly 1,600 air, water, soil and dust samples were taken beforehand to establish a baseline for measuring any potential environmental changes. Around five tons of degraded lead azide were destroyed after being deemed unsafe and unstable, and there were concerns that a plume of potentially toxic dust could drift towards Missouri in the wake of the blast. "Following the controlled detonation, EPA sampled homes, public parks with playgrounds, and every drinking water intake in the pre-detonation plume model. Today, EPA personnel and contractors will be specifically sampling schools, playgrounds, daycares, churches, and more in the region," the EPA said Thursday. "Extensive sampling of water in the Mississippi River watershed has been completed both before and after the controlled detonation." The EPA added that "air cassettes that sample for lead will be replaced to continue sampling today," and that "soil and dust sampling is expected to conclude today."
