articles.title: In 2021, Ashley Cain and Safiyya Vorajee lost their eight-month-old daughter and started a charity; five years later, it reports raising over £3 million and has funded treatment for children with cancer
articles.summary: What began as a heartbreaking loss has become the beginning of a mission to bring hope to families at their darkest hour.
articles.body: What began as a heartbreaking loss has become the beginning of a mission to bring hope to families at their darkest hour. Ashley Cain and Safiyya Vorajee are celebrating a poignant milestone through The Azaylia Foundation, which has raised over £3 million to help research, treat and improve outcomes for children diagnosed with cancer, five years after their daughter died from an aggressive form of childhood cancer.The Warwickshire-based charity was set up in 2021 in memory of their eight-month-old daughter, Azaylia Diamond Cain, and has turned personal tragedy into a sustained effort to address gaps in childhood cancer research and access to treatment.From mourning to a mission to changeAzaylia died in April 2021 of acute myeloid leukemia (AML). The foundation says her courage and determination through her illness inspired the creation of the Azaylia Foundation and continues to shape its work.The charity has raised more than £3 million since it was founded and has used the money to fund scientific research, institutional support and alternative treatment options for young patients, Warwickshire World says.One of the biggest drivers of its work is the limited funding for childhood cancer. The foundation said that fewer than 3 percent of research dollars for cancer go toward childhood cancers, in part because they are considered rare diseases.Research and early diagnosis investmentThe foundation has raised over £1m that has gone directly to research. Its contributions have supported seven PhD positions at four UK universities, including four at the University of Birmingham and one each at the universities of Oxford, East Anglia and Sheffield.The research programs aim to improve early diagnosis and more effective treatments for cancers in children. This could allow doctors to detect diseases earlier and provide better care.The foundation also supported scientific infrastructure. The University of Birmingham said it gave £120,000 to help buy a cell-sorting machine for cancer research led by Dr Francis Mussai. The equipment enables investigators to more efficiently isolate cancer cells from healthy blood and tissue cells, potentially speeding the development of new treatments.Supporting children to access alternative treatmentsAs well as research the charity has also set up Treatment Pathway Grants with other children’s hospital charities. The program allows specialist pediatric oncology consultants to explore alternative treatment pathways for children who have run out of standard NHS options.Warwickshire World reports the scheme has paid for private and international treatment for 20 children with cancer.A particularly heartening example is Yuvraj, who in June 2022 received £10,000 from the foundation to access Ruxolitinib after developing severe Graft Versus Host Disease following a stem cell transplant. He was not able to get the medication at the time through NHS funding.Four years on, Yuvraj has traveled a long way. He has gone back to school and has become a crusader for awareness with public appearances and media engagements.Azaylia’s legacy lives onAs The Azaylia Foundation turns five, its leadership is committed to driving up research funding, improving access to treatment and challenging inequalities in childhood cancer care.The charity is also planning further fundraising and advocacy activities, Warwickshire World reports.For Cain and Vorajee, the £3 million milestone is more than a fundraising achievement. It speaks to the continuing power of their daughter’s legacy and the opportunity to provide other families facing childhood cancer with something they once desperately needed: hope.Images Courtesy: Daily Mail and The SunYou use AI every day. articles.summary: JAMMU: A joint police team arrested a former terrorist wanted in a string of criminal cases from Tral in Awantipora district on Thursday, ending his
articles.body: JAMMU: A joint police team arrested a former terrorist wanted in a string of criminal cases from Tral in Awantipora district on Thursday, ending his nearly two-decade-long run from the law.The fugitive, Mohammad Mansha, is a native of Lassoli in Reasi district’s Thuroo tehsil. An active terrorist from 2000 to 2007, he was wanted in at least 13 criminal cases involving serious offences such as murder, attempted murder, criminal conspiracy, waging war against govt and Arms Act violations.He laid down arms in 2007, but managed to escape the law enforcement radar, continuing to evade arrest for the next 19 years, police said.Among the many cases in his name, Mansha was involved in the killing of a J&K Police SPO in 2000. He was charged under relevant sections of the RPC and the Arms Act, and declared an absconder after the chargesheet was submitted. A district and sessions court issued an arrest warrant against him in 2001.The joint operation involved sustained efforts, meticulous planning, and development of credible intelligence, a police spokesperson said. A special team from Mahore PS (Reasi) and the district absconder tracking unit was deputed to Tral. The team traced and arrested Mansha with assistance of Awantipora Police.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: The Macy’s Thanksgiving parade is postponed. What happens to its expansive roster of performers?
articles.summary: After bad weather postponed the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, a high school marching band that traveled from Texas to Manhattan for the annual festivities wondered what they were going to do.
articles.body: NEW YORK — After bad weather postponed the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade, a high school marching band that traveled from Texas to Manhattan for the annual festivities wondered what they were going to do. Staying in New York is notoriously expensive, even when a holiday isn’t driving up Midtown hotel costs. And then there’s the cost of feeding the 500 or so hungry kids who made the trip north. But in just a few hours after organizers moved the parade from Thursday to Saturday, the band from Pearland, Texas, managed to raise $350,000 to extend their stay for a few days, helped along by quick donations from businesses and almost 2,000 others. “I am still shocked at it, to be honest with you, I’m still shocked,” said Ryan Demkovich, the band’s director, who added that the news of the postponement broke while he and the band were watching the second act of a matinee showing of “Wicked” on Broadway. “We’re just very thankful for everybody that has just come together to really go above and beyond to make this a positive experience for everybody.” The band is just one of the parade’s expansive list of performers that are now changing plans, checking flight schedules and looking to extend hotel stays so they can stick around for the weekend. The parade was rescheduled as many wondered how its iconic balloons would handle powerful winds and rains bearing down on the city. It was the first time the parade has been postponed, Macy’s said, though it was canceled for three years during World War II. The retail giant said it was working with performers and trying to piece together the complex logistics of rescheduling the parade, which included deflating balloons and shelving them until Saturday. Performers for Broadway shows such as “The Rocky Horror Show,” “Wicked” and “Hamilton” will still make the new date, according to their representatives, as will the University of Connecticut’s marching band, which is set to perform in the parade for the first time. However, the University of Alabama’s Million Dollar Band will instead be heading home to perform at a football game. Meanwhile, the Nā Koa Aliʻi Hawaiʻi All-State Marching Band is hoping to scrape together around $700,000 so they can also remain in the city through Saturday and make it back home through an always hectic and costly season for traveling. “We are building that chest as we speak and it is trending and progressing, and we’re hopeful at this point, but you know, we’re just waiting,” said Rickey H Badua, the band’s director, who said they’re trying to accommodate a few hundred band members and staffers. “We’re waiting to see if people wake up with their families at home, if they see the message of need.” The city, following a severe balloon accident in 1997 that left a woman in a coma, has measures in place that dictate whether to lower balloons or nix them entirely if the wind is too strong. The parade balloons have been grounded only once due to weather, in 1971. The parade has long drawn tons of tourists to the city, and this year was no different, with Jess Rydell, 37, being just one who made her way to the Big Apple only to have her dreams of attending the event for the first time dashed in what she described as “a big letdown.” “Well, it is quite windy this morning so I think the balloons would have been grounded anyways, so it’s probably best for the safety of everyone, just disappointing when you’re here for it,” said Rydell, who instead tossed on a raincoat and strolled around Central Park.

articles.title: A garden fence dispute that began in 2012 spiralled into a 14-year neighbour feud involving an ornamental squirrel and offensive YouTube songs, leaving a couple with a £150,000 penalty
articles.summary: A couple have been ordered to pay around £150,000 after a 14-year feud with their neighbours over a garden fence escalated into a bitter legal battle
articles.body: A couple have been ordered to pay around £150,000 after a 14-year feud with their neighbours over a garden fence escalated into a bitter legal battle involving an ornamental squirrel and offensive YouTube songs. Philip New, 52, and his wife Denise, 47, faced court action from Steve and Karen Gibson after a disagreement over a fence allegedly being a few inches out of line. The dispute, which began in 2012, continued through multiple legal proceedings, with allegations of trespassing, distress and insulting behaviour. Despite appealing the damages awarded against them, the couple were handed a further £19,000 legal costs bill by the High Court.How a garden fence dispute sparked a 14-year neighbour feudThe disagreement began in 2012 when Philip New replaced several wooden fence panels separating the two properties. The Gibsons objected, arguing that the replacement fence had been installed in the wrong position and was not in a straight line. According to the Sun, the dispute concerned a boundary that the Gibsons believed should have been further inside the News' garden.The couple initially agreed to resolve their differences without going to court and appointed an independent surveyor in 2015 to establish the correct boundary. However, Mr and Mrs New disagreed with the line identified by the first expert and sought a second opinion. The disagreement eventually led to legal proceedings in 2018, with the court ruling in 2021 that the boundary identified by the original surveyor had to be followed. The News subsequently pursued a series of unsuccessful appeals.Ornamental squirrel row escalates the neighbour feudThe dispute extended beyond the position of the fence when Mr New removed an ornamental squirrel from a post standing between the properties. The incident happened shortly after the couple lost an appeal, and Mr Gibson told the court that the object had considerable sentimental value to his family. According to his statement, his parents-in-law had built the post after he purchased the squirrel as a gift for Mrs Gibson and her parents during the 1980s.Mr New subsequently removed the post itself using his hands and a mallet. He argued that he had taken it down because it was dangerous, but this explanation was rejected by the county court judge. In his judgment, Judge Robert Duddridge recorded the sentimental significance of the object and the distress caused by its removal. The squirrel incident formed part of the wider allegations about the conduct of the neighbours during the prolonged disagreement.Offensive YouTube songs add to 14-year neighbour feudThe court also heard about two songs, titled Neighbours and Magic Garden, which were discovered by one of the Gibsons' children in November 2020. The tracks had been published on YouTube and Facebook and were written by Mr New, who was described as a comedy songwriter. One of the songs, Neighbours, purported to offer advice on dealing with difficult neighbours and included lyrics encouraging listeners to throw waste at their windows and doors, use abusive language, and damage their property.The second song, Magic Garden, described a person who used walking sticks and appeared to be in pain in public but supposedly discarded the sticks and became pain-free when in their garden. It also made allegations of benefits fraud. Mr Gibson, who has a rare disability affecting his bones, said he found the song deeply upsetting and believed it was directed at him. Judge Duddridge said: "I am satisfied that the songs Neighbours and Magic Garden were directly about the Gibsons." He also described their content as offensive and defamatory, accepting that the songs had caused considerable embarrassment and emotional distress, particularly because of Mr Gibson's medical condition.14-year neighbour feud leaves couple with £150,000 penaltyFollowing the initial ruling at Southend County Court, the News were ordered to pay the Gibsons £13,305 in combined damages and interest, alongside legal costs estimated at around £120,000. The damages related to the fence trespassing on the neighbours' land, as well as distress, inconvenience and loss of enjoyment of their property. Judge Duddridge described the dispute as "unusually disproportionate, difficult and frustrating", saying it had "consumed" the neighbours' lives.The couple appealed to the High Court, arguing that the damages awarded against them were substantially too high and that the amount should be reduced sufficiently to overturn the costs order. However, Mr Justice Thompsell reduced the damages by just £700 and ordered them to pay a further nearly £19,000 towards the Gibsons' legal expenses for the appeal. He concluded that the neighbours had won the case in "substance and reality" and said the News' motivation for appealing had been to obtain a large enough reduction to avoid paying the other couple's legal costs. The final decision left Philip and Denise New facing a bill of around £150,000, including damages and legal expenses from the County Court and High Court proceedings.Disclaimer: This article is based on information publicly available from media reports and court proceedings. The Times of India has not independently verified all the allegations, statements or circumstances surrounding the neighbour dispute. The details reported should be understood in the context of the legal proceedings and the court's findings.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Egypt detains driver over Cairo fuel tanker fire that killed 31
articles.summary: Prosecutors order drug tests for the 21-year-old suspect, who says he was overtaking when the crash happened.
articles.body:
Prosecutors in Egypt have ordered the detention of a 21-year-old driver suspected of causing a collision on Wednesday that overturned a fuel tanker on Cairo’s ring road, starting a fire that killed 31 people .

The Public Prosecution announced on Thursday that it had ordered the man to be held pending an investigation, and sent him to the Forensic Medicine Authority for tests to determine whether he had taken drugs.

The tanker burst into flames at about 6:30pm (16:30 GMT) on Wednesday, at the height of the evening rush hour, on an elevated stretch of the ring road in al-Waraq, a densely populated district of Giza on the western edge of the capital. The fire spread to passing traffic and destroyed 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles.

In an earlier statement, prosecutors said the driver told investigators he had been travelling from al-Marg towards al-Haram at 110km/h (68mph), with his father in the car, and was switching lanes to overtake other vehicles when the front left of his car struck the rear right of the tanker.

The man told prosecutors he then lost control and his car veered to the far right of the road. One of the tanker’s tyres burst, the statement said, before the vehicle hit a concrete barrier and overturned. Petrol leaking from the truck caught fire.

Prosecutors said they identified the driver after inspecting the scene and interviewing witnesses, and had since spoken to all the injured whose condition allowed them to be questioned. Forensic teams are taking DNA samples from victims’ relatives to identify some of the bodies. Relatives posted appeals on Facebook for men who had been on the road and had not been heard from since, the Reuters news agency reported.

The investigation will determine whether the driver bears criminal responsibility.

The Ministry of Health and Population on Thursday put the final toll at 31 dead and 26 injured, up from the 21 injured it had reported on Wednesday. Five of the injured have left hospital. The other 21 are still being treated, including eight transferred to other hospitals for further care. The bodies of the dead are in the custody of prosecutors, the ministry said.

By Thursday morning, traffic was moving again after crews cleared most of the burned wreckage. Salah Ahmed, a microbus driver, told the AP news agency that he had been on the ring road when the tanker caught fire but was held back by traffic, which saved his life.

“It was God’s hellfire on the ring road,” he said. “Why is a truck like this on the ring road at a rush hour? Who gets penalised for this happening?”

A 2018 cabinet decision barred trucks carrying more than four tonnes from the ring road between 6am and midnight, the AFP news agency reported. Prosecutors have not said why the tanker was on the road at the time.

“The tanks were exploding, the tyres were exploding, and there was fire,” Zaghlol al-Me, a local resident who reached the scene shortly after the crash, told Reuters. “We just didn’t know what to do or how to save anyone.”

The Public Prosecution’s statements are the first official account of how the crash happened. Early reports in local media suggested that a high-voltage cable had fallen in front of the tanker. On Wednesday night, the Ministry of Transport denied issuing any statement to that effect and said the cause was a matter for prosecutors.

The Ministry of Electricity and Renewable Energy said the overhead lines were taut when the fire began and that two circuits tripped only after it started. The ministry’s spokesman, Mansour Abdel Ghani, told the Egyptian Youm7 daily newspaper that the lines had no connection to the crash and melted in the heat. A high-voltage line lay twisted on the ground on Thursday, AP reported.

President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi ordered full medical care for the injured and support for the families of those killed. Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly visited the injured on Thursday with Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar and Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy. Madbouly said the government, civil society and businesspeople would provide bank investment certificates to give bereaved families a stable income, and replacement vehicles for people whose cars burned.

“We realise that no compensation or money can make up for those we have lost,” Madbouly said.

Egypt’s Ministry of Social Solidarity said on Thursday that people could donate through the InstaPay app to help the injured and the families of those killed. It also opened an account at Nasser Social Bank for donations from businesses and civil society groups. The cabinet said the ministry had received 24 million Egyptian pounds (about $445,000) from seven charities.

The crash has renewed questions about road safety in Egypt. The Ministry of Transport says it spent about $37bn on transport between 2014 and 2024, yet 5,829 people were killed on the country’s roads in 2025, up 10.8 percent from the year before, and about 84,000 were injured, according to the state statistics agency, CAPMAS.

Egyptian legislators demanded accountability on Thursday. Mahmoud Samy, an MP, said the government needed to move from “building roads and expanding them to managing their safety professionally”. Abdel Moneim Imam, a politician who chairs the liberal Justice Party, said the cabinet bore full responsibility and should resign.

Amr Moussa, Egypt’s former foreign minister and former secretary-general of the Arab League, also criticised what he described as a deterioration in government oversight.

“Trading accusations and evading responsibility leads to the next disaster,” Moussa said, according to Reuters.

Transport Minister Kamel al-Wazir was appointed in 2019 after a train crash at Cairo’s Ramses station triggered a fire that killed 25 people, according to Reuters. He has rejected calls to resign since then, including after a lorry crash in the Nile Delta that killed 19 people, almost all of them young women, last year. The ministry declined to comment further when contacted by Reuters.

Earlier this month, a train crash, also in Giza, killed at least seven people and injured more than 125, prompting calls from legislators for accountability over recurring transport accidents.

articles.title: UK shields fighter jets, contacts reservists in Cold War-scale push amid Russia threat
articles.summary: Wes Streeting says the United Kingdom is contacting former service members to update its strategic reserve as Russian sabotage rises across Europe.
articles.body: The United Kingdom is bolstering its military readiness amid growing threats from Russia, contacting former service members to assess its reserves as the Royal Air Force reportedly strengthens defenses against potential drone attacks. Britain's Ministry of Defence has written to former service members to verify their contact information and military skills to ensure the country is prepared for a national emergency or potential conflict, Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting confirmed Friday. The outreach comes as the International Institute for Strategic Studies warned Thursday that suspected Russian-directed sabotage across Europe could trigger a "mass-casualty event." NATO WARNS PUTIN COULD STRIKE BEFORE EUROPEAN ARMY RESPONDS, POINTS TO US AS MILITARY MODEL The think tank found that sabotage incidents rose 16% in the year through September 2026, with Germany and Poland accounting for more than half of the cases. Researchers warned that a major attack could spark calls for retaliation and divide European governments. "I want the country to be alert, not alarmed," Streeting told BBC Radio 4's "Today" program. "You can't not look at what's going on in Europe and not be concerned about a threat environment which has deteriorated in recent years and is sadly increasing," he said. Streeting said the government needed updated records of its strategic reserve in case former service members were called upon to respond to a domestic disaster or overseas conflict. He cited Russian incursions into Polish airspace, suspected Russian-sponsored sabotage across Europe and Iran-linked threats to British military bases. Last week, a suspected Russian projectile landed in eastern Poland about 60 miles from a British-led military exercise. The incident happened the same day Britain's defense secretary and chief of the air staff visited troops. INSIDE THE PENTAGON'S DOOMSDAY PLAN TO KEEP AMERICA FIGHTING IF GLOBAL WAR ERUPTS "And so against that backdrop, against that threat environment, the government and the country has to be ready to face down those risks," Streeting said. "Because the more ready we are, the less likely we are to find ourselves in a conflict, in a war. That is my goal. That is the goal of this government." The Ministry of Defence said in a news release it was contacting thousands of former military personnel this week as part of a drive to "strengthen the UK’s readiness and deliver on recommendations made in the Strategic Defence Review." "Service Chiefs are writing to members of the Strategic Reserve, asking them to stay connected and update their details, providing Defence with a better understanding of the skills and experience it could draw upon if needed." "In the coming months, Strategic Reservists will have the opportunity to volunteer for training and exercises, such as the UK’s participation in NATO’s flagship Steadfast Defender next spring." The outreach marks the first time since the Cold War that Britain's defense ministry has contacted reservists on such a scale to encourage participation in military exercises, according to The Telegraph. TRUMP’S PROPOSED RUSSIA DEAL RAISES NATO ALARM AS EX-COMMANDER WARNS PUTIN SEEKS INFLUENCE OVER EUROPE Meanwhile, Britain's domestic intelligence agency, MI5, and the defense ministry have reportedly warned British companies supplying military equipment to Ukraine that they could be targeted by Russian saboteurs. The Royal Air Force is strengthening security at military bases, using hardened aircraft shelters and installing anti-drone netting to protect exposed fighter jets, according to The Times. The measures follow Iranian threats against military bases in England that prompted tighter security and the relocation of U.S. military aircraft. Suspected drone incursions over European airfields have also heightened concerns about Russian aggression. "We take the security of our bases, equipment and personnel very seriously and are always adapting to counter any potential threats," a Ministry of Defence spokesperson told Fox News Digital. US MILITARY BASES ARE ‘ILL-EQUIPPED’ TO STOP DRONE SWARMS, TOP COMMANDER REVEALS AFTER RUBIO'S UAP WARNING "This includes investing an additional £470 million to strengthen security at military sites, including better physical protection, surveillance and counter-drone capabilities. "We have already invested £15 million in drone and counter-drone technology and introduced restricted airspace over 44 critical Defence sites." The developments come as President Donald Trump said Thursday he had asked Russian President Vladimir Putin to "pull back all military aggression" against Europe, signaling a shift in tone toward the Russian leader, whom he called a friend last week. Trump said he made the request during a meeting with Putin in China last week, adding that he believed it could help secure a deal to end Russia's war in Ukraine. Trump's comments came a day after he hosted NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte in Florida. The two leaders issued a joint statement urging Russia not to expand its war in Ukraine. articles.title: In 1712, a Dutch East India Company ship sank off Western Australia with thousands of silver coins; 314 years later, 23 coins stolen from its wreck have returned from California and Amsterdam after an international investigation
articles.summary: A shipwreck that lay beneath the waters off Western Australia for more than three centuries has become the centre of an international investigation, with
articles.body: A shipwreck that lay beneath the waters off Western Australia for more than three centuries has become the centre of an international investigation, with 23 silver coins stolen from its seabed finally returning to Australia. The coins, taken from the Dutch East India Company vessel Zuytdorp, were recovered in the Netherlands and the United States and formally handed back to Australian authorities on November 24, 2026, according to a joint media release by the Australian government and a report by ABC News.The Zuytdorp disappeared in 1712 while travelling from the Netherlands to Batavia, now Jakarta, carrying a valuable cargo that included 128,000 Dutch guilders worth of silver coins. The ship sank off the coast of Western Australia, between Kalbarri and Shark Bay, in circumstances that remain unknown. Around 200 people were aboard, but unlike the crews of some other Dutch vessels wrecked along the coast, the Zuytdorp's survivors were never heard from again.The wreck's location remained a mystery for centuries. In 1927, a young geologist discovered Dutch silver coins and other artefacts near the cliffs that later came to be known as the Zuytdorp Cliffs. The objects were eventually linked to the missing ship. In 1964, local divers Tom Brady and brothers Graham and Max Cramer explored the waters below the cliffs and found the wreck, including sections of its hull, cannons and anchors. Thousands of silver coins were scattered across the seabed.The coins were more than just valuable cargo. Their dates helped researchers establish when the ship could have sunk. Western Australian Museum head of maritime heritage Corioli Souter told ABC News that the earliest possible date for the wreck was 1711, based on the coins' minting dates. She described the site as important national cultural heritage that belongs to the people of Australia.However, the wreck's remote location and difficult sea conditions did little to deter treasure hunters. Over the decades, hundreds of coins were removed illegally from the seabed. The Western Australian Museum became legally responsible for the site in 1969 and began recovering coins to prevent further looting. A watchman was stationed near the cliffs during the 1970s, but surveillance ended after his caravan was firebombed. Salvage work was also interrupted by dangerous conditions before resuming in 1986.The latest investigation began after Australian authorities noticed a sharp rise in permit requests involving Zuytdorp coins between 2019 and 2021. The unusual interest raised concerns that artefacts had been illegally removed and were circulating among collectors. The National Environmental Protection Agency led the Australian investigation, working with the United States Federal Bureau of Investigation, the Netherlands National Police, local law enforcement and underwater cultural heritage experts. Dutch authorities seized two coins in Amsterdam in November 2024 at Australia's request. The coins had surfaced at an auction in the Netherlands after being illegally brought overseas. The FBI later led inquiries in California, locating and securing 21 more coins.The 23 coins were formally returned to Assistant Minister Josh Wilson at the National EPA in Canberra by representatives of the Netherlands and the United States. The Australian government said it was the first time stolen Australian underwater cultural heritage taken overseas had been returned following a criminal investigation.The international recovery was part of a broader effort to trace artefacts taken from the wreck. Searches in the Geraldton area in late 2024 and early 2025 recovered dozens of coins. Geraldton man Ashley Patterson pleaded guilty in August to four offences under Australia's Underwater Cultural Heritage Act 2018 and is due to be sentenced early next year. The law prohibits possessing, supplying or exporting protected underwater cultural heritage without a permit. The maximum penalty is five years' imprisonment and/or a fine of A$99,000.The recovered coins will ultimately return to Western Australia, where the WA Shipwrecks Museum in Fremantle will conserve and care for them. Australia and the Netherlands have also renewed an agreement to collaborate on researching and protecting their shared underwater heritage.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Supreme Court to banks: Give nod to try officials in 7 days
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has read out the riot act and asked HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital and PNB Home Finance to grant unconditional
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Supreme Court has read out the riot act and asked HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank, Sammaan Capital and PNB Home Finance to grant unconditional sanction within a week to prosecute their bank officials, who are charged by CBI for colluding with builders in the alleged duping of homebuyers under the subvention schemes, or remain present in court to explain the lapse.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati said CBI, as directed by the SC, had inquired into 55 cases pan-India and has filed chargesheets in 22 cases, closed 3 cases and expects to complete the probe into the rest in three months.Once sanction is granted, courts will expeditiously take cognisance of CBI chargesheets, start trial: SCBhati informed a bench of CJI Surya Kant, Justice Joymalay Bagchi and V Mohana that in the 22 cases, HDFC, ICICI, Samman and PNB have granted conditional sanction for prosecution, which is creating doubts in the minds of trial courts in taking cognisance of the chargesheet and proceeding with framing of charges.When senior advocate Sanjiv Sen, appearing for HDFC, said that sanction has been granted but there are certain rulings of the constitutional courts that flag the issue of whether private bank officials are public servants requiring sanction for prosecution. Moreover, the officials charged have been exonerated of wrongdoing in the internal inquiry, Sen said.The CJI-led bench said what else but exoneration of officials is expected in internal inquiries by banks, which had hobnobbed with rogue builders and cheated the homebuyers by releasing large sums of loan instalments to the builders even when there was hardly any progress in the construction of housing projects.When Sen protested against grant of sanction citing a judgment, the bench differentiated and said this is a court-monitored investigation, and hence SC can direct the banks to grant unconditional sanction for prosecution of delinquent officials.The bench said, “We direct all banks to issue unconditional sanction for prosecution within a week, failing which their CMDs shall remain present in court to explain why action should not be taken against them.”The bench said once the sanction is granted, the trial courts will expeditiously take cognisance of CBI chargesheets and begin trial as per law. It also directed CBI to conclude investigations into the remaining cases expeditiously and not later than two months.On Aug 6, SC said that in court-monitored investigations, sanction for prosecution should be granted promptly and directed the banks to give necessary permissions within two weeks for prosecution of the accused bank officials. “Failure to accord sanction within two weeks would require banks to submit explanations to the court,” it had said and asked the CBI to share documents on the money trail with the ED to kick off an inquiry under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 'Horrible spike' in flu warning as hospital admissions surge
articles.summary: Health officials are urging those at risk of getting flu to get vaccinated as soon as possible.
articles.body:
A surge in severe cases of flu has prompted health officials in England to urge those most at risk to get vaccinated as soon as possible.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) said hospital admission rates had soared by almost 80% over the last week to the highest at this time of year since before the Covid pandemic.

Flu vaccine uptake so far among those aged 65 and over is just under 68% - lower than where it usually is at this time of year, the agency said. The flu can be very serious for those living with some long term health conditions.

Outgoing chief executive for NHS England, Sir Jim Mackey, said how some hospitals have introduced mask-wearing to stem the spread of respiratory illnesses.

Winter flu vaccine rollout begins. Who's eligible?

Are max strength cold and flu pills worth the money?

Speaking at the NHS Alliance autumn conference, Sir Jim said he was asked to wear a mask for the first time in years during a hospital visit, saying it was "a bit of a shock".

"I think we have more beds occupied with flu than we did this time last year, as we're just about going to that horrible spike in flu," he said.

According to the UKHSA, almost 9.5 million people under the age of 65 in clinical risk groups - including those with lung conditions, kidney or liver disease and diabetes - are eligible for the flu jab.

However, only 34% had received a flu vaccine up to 22 November, leaving almost 7 million without vital protection.

Sir Jim also condemned corridor care in hospitals saying that it had become "embedded" in some parts of the health service.

"It's not something any of us would want for our families, our mothers, our aunties, uncles – whether it's from a safety point of view, or more importantly from a personal dignity point of view," he said, adding there was a need to get a grip and eliminate it.

UKHSA flu lead Dr Suzanna McDonald told the BBC that the sharp rise in flu cases was happening earlier compared to last winter and previous flu seasons.

"Flu is very, very unpredictable and we don't know what the flu season will look like until it has unfolded," she said, adding that although last year's flu season arrived early, it peaked at "moderate levels".

She said it is not known if this flu season will go on for longer, or peak higher, but urged people to get vaccinated, saying said thousands of people die from the flu every year.

However, flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practice good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 37% of those eligible have taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies until 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives".

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

articles.title: ME sufferers and families need more help, campaigner says
articles.summary: Shauna Chambers said her partner Row was “full of energy” but now cannot tolerate light or noise.
articles.body:
Rowena Davies had been planning to travel the world with her partner until an ME diagnosis left her unable to talk or leave her bed.

The 42-year-old, known as Row, initially thought she was burnt out, but after years of searching for answers was finally diagnosed in 2021 and her partner Shauna Chambers has since given up work to help the family care for her.

Campaigners are warning that people with severe ME - sometimes referred to clinically as myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome - could die without changes to services in Wales.

The Welsh government said proposals for an all‑Wales specialist, an expert group and national standards were being considered.

It is estimated more than 400,000 people across the UK have ME, a complex multi-system condition with no known cure.

Shauna, 34, said: "She had a cough that didn't leave for many months, but the main thing was that she would be absolutely drained and exhausted after doing such small things.

"Now, she really isn't able to do anything at all."

Shauna, from Tywyn in Gwynedd, said Row was "full of energy" and loved sport, but now she cannot tolerate light or noise, and any exertion will cause her to deteriorate.

"We feed her, we wash her, we brush her teeth. We were left to navigate this on our own," she said.

"It's like you're grieving someone that is still alive, and you sit next to her sometimes, and all you can do is just hold her hand and breathe.

"People's lives have been completely ruined by this condition, and if nothing changes people can die from ME, and it is absolutely avoidable."

Campaigners told BBC Wales in March that healthcare services were "like a desert" for those most severely affected.

With the right support, Row's family are hopeful she can get better. She recently had her first visit by the Living Well service within Betsi Cadwaladr health board, which has been expanded to include ME, and now aims to support people living with any severity of the condition.

It uses funding from the Welsh government's Adferiad programme but campaigners say that services vary between health boards. There is no clinical lead for ME in Wales.

John Peters, 65, from Swansea, was diagnosed with the condition 40 years ago. He was once a keen rugby player, but after a virus, his life changed.

"I would rest for a couple of days which would sort of take the edge off it, and then I'd sort of go at it again, and it would make it worse," he explained.

He now describes the effects as being mild to moderate, but he has spent periods of his life lying in a dark room for days on end.

"I've gone through improvements, and then got another infection, and that's been the cycle of my life since 1985," he said.

"One of the hardest things is the loss of identity. You're not a husband, a father, you don't have a career.

"Your life goes past and then you realise what's happened. I hate the illness.

"No one knows what I've been through. There is no care for me."

Swansea Bay University Health Board said its service, also funded by the Adferiad programme, "focuses on improving quality of life, supporting independence, and enabling individuals to manage the impact of ME within their own daily circumstances" while "recognising the fluctuating nature of the condition and the importance of personalised care".

ME is a chronic and complex multi-system condition, which causes symptoms such as extreme fatigue and post-exertional malaise.

That means simple physical or mental activities can leave people completely debilitated.

Not everyone with ME is affected in the same way. There is a spectrum of severity, which is often categorised as mild, moderate, severe and very severe.

While researchers are still investigating the causes, triggers may include infection or other illness. There is no specific treatment.

Liverpool-based private consultant Dr Binita Kane, who has a special interest in ME and long Covid, said she had a growing waiting list of patients across the UK.

"I think that is a sad reflection on the fact that the services, sadly, don't exist at the moment in the way they need to through the NHS," she said.

"Even if patients can access a service, they often can't access medications and treatments for symptom control and support for overlapping conditions because there aren't doctors integrated into those services."

She said the goal is always "to prevent people from getting into the very severe state" through early intervention, but she said that certain investigations can happen at people's homes, such as 24-hour ECG tests, sleep studies and blood tests.

"People sadly do die from severe ME for different reasons, it is a risk, and ME is one of the only conditions I'm aware of where the more sick you are, the less access to treatment and help and support you get," she added.

"These are young people whose lives have been decimated, destroyed, who aren't getting enough help, care, and support.

"There's a million reasons why the government should be taking this extremely seriously."

Campaign groups in Wales have joined together to call on the government to bring together a national expert group, appoint an all-Wales clinical lead, and develop a research strategy.

In a recent survey of more than 5,400 people across the UK, 62.1% of respondents in Wales reported having no NHS specialist ME service in their area, compared with 32.8% in England.

Action for ME, who conducted the survey, said the findings demonstrate that "access to specialist care remains a postcode lottery".

"People have been waiting for decades and that is too long" said the charity's chief executive Sonya Chowdhury.

She said that a cross-party debate was held in the Senedd in December 2025 in which the current health minister, Plaid Cymru's Mabon ap Gwynfor MS, advocated on behalf of ME patients while in opposition.

"We are 12 months on, and we are yet to see action," she added.

"It's fantastic that the minister has met with us and other groups here in Wales, and we have heard some positive noises, but what we need to see now is something changing."

A Welsh government spokesperson said it's "working to improve support for people living with post-infection associated chronic illness, including ME, and recognise that more needs to be done".

"We have met with groups representing people with ME and long Covid. We aim to provide an update in due course," it added.

"Through Adferiad, we provide £8m a year to develop services and specialist clinical expertise to support people with long-term conditions, including ME."
